summary: Describes the format and publication mechanisms IANA uses to distribute the DNSSEC trust anchors for the root zone, which clients need to validate DNSSEC answers. It obsoletes RFC 7958.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC lets a resolver check that a DNS answer has not been altered. The check starts from a key that the resolver simply believes, called a trust anchor, and for the whole Internet that anchor is the root zone key published by IANA. This RFC defines the file IANA publishes, what each field in it means, and the two ways a program can check that the file really came from IANA.

questions: where to get the dnssec root trust anchor
how iana publishes root zone trust anchors
what is a dnssec trust anchor
where is the dns root trust anchor published
subtitle: How IANA publishes the DNSSEC trust anchors that every validating DNS resolver needs.

tldr.problem: A DNS resolver that wants to check signatures has to start somewhere, and that starting point is the root zone key. Someone has to publish that key in a form that software can read and that a user can check.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an XML document that holds the hashes of the root zone signing keys, together with the times each hash is valid, and it defines where the file lives and how its origin can be checked.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document that obsoletes RFC 7958. It drops the old self-signed PGP message and self-issued certificate method in favour of a signature chaining to an ICANN certificate authority and to the ordinary web PKI.

facts.label: Signature format
facts.value: A detached Cryptographic Message Syntax signature chaining to the ICANN certificate authority

facts.label: Root zone indication
facts.value: A single period character in the Zone element

today: RFC 9718 was published in January 2025 as an Informational document and obsoletes RFC 7958. It has not been obsoleted or updated since. The document removes the old self-signed PGP message and self-issued certificate signing request as distribution methods, and adds an optional public key and flags to the trust anchor entries.

sections.title: Why a Trust Anchor Is Published
sections.content:
The global Domain Name System is described in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and DNS Security Extensions are described in RFC 9364. In the DNSSEC protocol, Resource Record Sets are signed cryptographically, so a response to a query contains signatures that allow the integrity and authenticity of the record set to be verified. Those signatures are validated by following a chain of signatures to a trust anchor. The reason for trusting a trust anchor is outside the DNSSEC protocol, but having one or more trust anchors is required for the protocol to work at all.

The publication of trust anchors for the root zone of the DNS is an IANA function performed by ICANN through its affiliate Public Technical Identifiers. The document describes the formats and distribution methods of the DNSSEC trust anchors that IANA uses for the root zone. Other organizations might have different formats and mechanisms for distributing root zone trust anchors, but most operators and software vendors have chosen to rely on the IANA trust anchors.

On terminology, the RFC notes that the term trust anchor is used in many different contexts in the security community, and that many of the common definitions conflict because they are specific to one system, such as just DNSSEC or just S/MIME messages. In cryptographic systems with hierarchical structure, a trust anchor is an authoritative entity for which trust is assumed and not derived. The format of the entity differs between systems, but all common uses share the basic idea that the decision to trust this entity is made outside the system that relies on it. The RFC notes that the formats defined here do not match the definition of trust anchor given in RFC 4033, a configured DNSKEY record or DS record hash of a DNSKEY record, but a system that wants to convert the trusted material from IANA into a Delegation Signer record can do so.

The formats and distribution methods are a complement to, not a substitute for, the automated trust anchor update protocol of RFC 5011. That protocol allows secure in-band succession of trust anchors once trust has already been established, while this document describes one way to establish an initial trust anchor that the mechanism of RFC 5011 can use. This document obsoletes RFC 7958.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC works by checking a chain of signatures upwards until it reaches a key that is trusted for its own sake. For the whole Internet that key is the root zone signing key, and IANA is the body that publishes it. The RFC is about how that one key gets from IANA to the resolvers that need it, and how they can tell they got the genuine article.

sections.title: The XML Format and What Each Field Means
sections.content:
IANA publishes trust anchors for the root zone as an XML document that contains the hashes of the DNSKEY records and optionally the keys from those records. The hashes are consistent with the defined presentation format of a Delegation Signer resource, and the keys and flags are consistent with the presentation format of a DNSKEY resource. The hashes are mandatory in the syntax, but the keys are optional. The XML document can carry XML comments, which IANA might use to add pointers to important information on its website; the comments are only human-readable commentary, not extensions to the grammar.

The schema is given as RELAX NG Compact. The TrustAnchor element is the container for all the trust anchors in the file, and it holds an id attribute, which is an opaque string identifying the set of trust anchors with no particular semantics, a source attribute, which gives information about where to obtain the container and is likely to be a URL but is advisory only, a Zone element stating which DNS zone the container applies to in presentation format including the trailing dot, with the root zone indicated by a single period character, and one or more KeyDigest elements.

Each KeyDigest element represents the digest of a past, current or potential future DNSKEY record of the zone named in the Zone element. Its own id attribute is an opaque string identifying the hash, and it is different from the id attribute of the enclosing TrustAnchor element. The validFrom and validUntil attributes specify the range of times in which the element can be used as a trust anchor; validUntil is optional. The KeyTag element holds the key tag for the DNSKEY record represented in the KeyDigest, the Algorithm element holds the DNSSEC signing algorithm identifier for that record, the DigestType element holds the DNSSEC digest algorithm identifier for it, and the Digest element holds the hexadecimal representation of the hash for it.

The optional publickeyinfo pattern inside a KeyDigest contains two mandatory elements: the base64 representation of the public key for the DNSKEY record and the flags of that record. It is new in this specification, and it can be useful when IANA has a trust anchor that has not yet been published in the DNS root, and for calculating a comparison to the Digest element.
sections.plainLanguage: The file is XML. One element holds the whole set and names the zone it is for, which for the root is a single dot. Inside it, each key digest says which key it refers to, when that key may be used, and what its hash is. The key itself and its flags may also be included, and that is new in this version of the document.

sections.title: An Example Trust Anchor File
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example of what the trust anchor file might look like, noting that the full public key is only given for a trust anchor that does not have a validFrom time in the past. The example holds three KeyDigest elements: one whose validUntil time is in the past, with key tag 19036; one with key tag 20326 and validFrom 2017-02-02, which includes the public key and the flags 257; and one called KSK-2024 as a shorthand name, with key tag 38696 and validFrom 2024-07-18, which carries only the digest.

From that example the RFC derives the Delegation Signer record set, which has two records, for key tags 20326 and 38696, both with algorithm 8 and digest type 2. A potential third record, one that includes key tag 19036, is already invalid because of the validUntil value and is therefore not part of the trust anchor set.

The derived DNSKEY record set has only one record, because a potential second record based on key tag 19036 is already invalid, and a potential second record based on key tag 38696 does not contain the optional publickeyinfo pattern and so its DNSKEY record cannot be calculated.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example shows why the extra fields matter. One of the three keys has expired and is excluded, so the file yields two usable delegation signer records. A third key is present in the file but has no key material in it, so a program that wanted the DNSKEY record rather than the hash could not produce one for it.

sections.title: How the File Is Retrieved and Checked
sections.content:
Trust anchors are available for retrieval using HTTPS and HTTP. The URL for retrieving the set of hashes in the XML document is the root-anchors.xml file on data.iana.org. If HTTPS cannot be used, the scheme is replaced with http.

A validator operator can choose whether or not to accept the trust anchors described in the document, using whatever policy they want. To help operators verify the content and origin of the trust anchors they receive, IANA uses digital signatures that chain to an ICANN-controlled certificate authority over the trust anchor data. It is important to note that the ICANN certificate authority is not a DNSSEC trust anchor; it is an optional mechanism for verifying the content and origin of the XML and certificate trust anchors.

Two mechanisms are described. The content and origin of the XML document can be verified using a digital signature on the file: IANA provides a detached Cryptographic Message Syntax signature that chains to the ICANN certificate authority with the XML document, which can be useful for validator operators who have received a copy of that authority's public key in a trusted out-of-band fashion, and the URL for that detached signature is the root-anchors.p7s file on data.iana.org. The other method is the use of the Transport Layer Security protocol for distributing the trust anchors: the certificate authority used for data.iana.org is currently well known, in that it is a WebTrust-accredited authority, so if a system retrieving the trust anchors trusts that authority, HTTPS should be used instead of HTTP in order to have assurance of data origin.

The trust model has changed. IANA used to distribute trust anchors as a self-signed Pretty Good Privacy message and as a self-issued certificate signing request, as described in RFC 7958. This document removes those methods because they rely on a trust model that mixes out-of-band trust of authentication keys with out-of-band trust of the DNSSEC root keys. Cryptographic assurance for the contents of the trust anchor now comes from the web PKI or the ICANN certificate authority, and that assurance is bolstered by informal comparisons made by users of the trust anchors, such as software vendors comparing the trust anchor files they are using.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two files to fetch, the anchors themselves and a detached signature over them. A program that already trusts the certificate authority behind data.iana.org can simply use HTTPS. A program that wants an independent check can fetch the signature and check it against a copy of the ICANN authority's public key it obtained by some other route. The older method of a self-signed PGP message is dropped, because it needed two separate acts of trust and only proved one.

sections.title: Security Considerations for Relying Parties
sections.content:
The document describes how DNSSEC trust anchors for the root zone are published, and notes that many DNSSEC clients will only configure IANA-issued trust anchors for the DNS root to perform validation, so reliable publication of trust anchors is important. Some of the methods described have different security properties, and users of the trust anchor file need to consider these when choosing whether to load the set of trust anchors.

The body of the document does not specify any particular behaviour for relying parties, and in particular does not say how a relying party should treat the trust anchor file as a whole, but some of its contents require particular attention.

On validUntil, the attribute is optional. If the relying party is using a trust anchor whose KeyDigest has no validUntil attribute, it can change to a trust anchor whose KeyDigest does have one, as long as that validUntil is in the future and the KeyTag, Algorithm, DigestType and Digest elements are the same as before. Relying parties should not use a KeyDigest outside of the time range given in the validFrom and validUntil attributes.

On comparing the digest and the public key information, if the Digest element would not be a proper delegation signer record for the DNSKEY record represented by the publickeyinfo pattern, relying parties must not use that KeyDigest as a trust anchor, and a party that wants to make such a comparison needs to marshal the elements of the DNSKEY record that became the delegation signer record using the algorithm specified in RFC 4034.

Two warnings follow. Relying parties need to implement trust anchor matching carefully, because a single trust anchor represented by a KeyDigest element can change its Digest and KeyTag values between two versions of the file, for example when the key is revoked or the flag value changes; parties that fail to take this into account are at risk of using an incorrect set of trust anchors. And because relying parties that require the optional publickeyinfo pattern to create trust anchors will store fewer trust anchors than those that only require a Digest element, two systems processing the same trust anchor file can end up with a different set of trust anchors.
sections.plainLanguage: The file can hold keys that are not usable yet, keys that have expired and keys that are in between. A program that ignores the validity dates, or that assumes a key keeps the same identifier between releases of the file, can end up trusting the wrong set of keys. The RFC also notes that two programs reading the same file may end up with different sets, simply because one of them insists on having the key material and the other does not.

viz.caption: WHAT EACH FIELD OF A KEYDIGEST CARRIES

items.title: id
items.text: An opaque string that identifies the hash. It is not the same thing as the id of the enclosing TrustAnchor element.

items.title: validFrom and validUntil
items.text: The range of times in which the KeyDigest can be used as a trust anchor. The validUntil attribute is optional.

items.title: KeyTag
items.text: The key tag for the DNSKEY record the KeyDigest represents.

items.title: Algorithm
items.text: The DNSSEC signing algorithm identifier for that DNSKEY record.

items.title: DigestType
items.text: The DNSSEC digest algorithm identifier for that DNSKEY record.

items.title: Digest
items.text: The hexadecimal representation of the hash for that DNSKEY record.

items.title: publickeyinfo
items.text: Optional and new in this specification. The base64 public key and the flags of the DNSKEY record.
